common_name: Saturn Peach (Donut Peach, Low-Chill White Flat Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Saturn has an unusually low chill requirement of only about 200-300 hours below 45F, so it blooms and fruits reliably in mild-winter Gulf Coast gardens where standard round-fruited peaches often fail to break dormancy evenly; self-fertile, no pollinizer needed.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil amended with compost; Saturn is self-fruitful and needs no second tree for pollination. This is the donut- or saucer-shaped 'flat peach' long grown in China and more recently popularized in the U.S. by Dave Wilson Nursery under the Saturn name; the fruit is squashed-looking with a sunken center, white-fleshed, low in acid, and sweet with a mild almond-like note. Because its chill requirement is so low (roughly 200-300 hours), Saturn sets a reliable crop in zone 9-10 Gulf Coast gardens where many classic round peaches bloom erratically after warm winters; thin fruit to 4-6 inches apart after June drop to size up the remaining crop, and watch for brown rot and plum curculio in humid climates. Prune annually to an open center to maintain airflow through the canopy, which helps control fungal disease pressure typical of the humid Southeast.
sources: Dave Wilson Nursery — Peach Variety Database
California Rare Fruit Growers — Peach Fruit Facts
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Home Fruit Production

common_name: O'Henry Peach (Large Red-Skinned California Commercial Freestone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; O'Henry requires about 750 chill hours, placing it in the moderate-to-high range for peaches, so it is best suited to zones 5-9 rather than the Deep South's mildest winters; self-fertile.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; O'Henry is self-fruitful and vigorous, producing heavy crops of large, firm, 70-80% red-blushed yellow freestone fruit over a long harvest window in late summer. Thin fruit early to 4-6 inches apart to prevent limb breakage and improve size and sugar content; this variety is a mainstay of the California commercial fresh and processing peach industry because of its shipping quality, but it performs equally well in home orchards where its 750-hour chill requirement can be met. Watch for peach leaf curl in wet spring weather and apply a dormant copper spray if the disease has been a problem in previous years.
sources: Dave Wilson Nursery — Peach Variety Database

common_name: Candor Peach (Early-Season Bacterial Spot-Resistant NC State Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Candor has a flexible chill requirement (roughly 350-900 hours depending on source) and is valued for ripening about three weeks ahead of Redhaven with good resistance to bacterial spot; self-fertile.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil in a site with good air drainage to minimize frost damage to the early bloom; Candor is self-fruitful and vigorous. Introduced by North Carolina State University's peach breeding program in 1965, Candor remains valued today as one of the earliest-ripening peaches of real eating quality, bearing medium-sized, 75-80% red-blushed yellow clingstone fruit about 20 days before Redhaven. Its resistance to bacterial spot — a serious foliage and fruit disease in the humid Southeast — makes it a dependable choice for home orchards in the Carolinas and similar humid-summer climates; thin fruit after bloom to improve size.
sources: NC State Extension — Peach Cultivars for the Home Orchard
Clemson Cooperative Extension — Home Garden Peaches

common_name: Julyprince Peach (USDA-ARS Byron Georgia Large Firm Freestone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Julyprince was released in 2008 by USDA-ARS at Byron, Georgia and carries a moderate-to-high chill requirement typical of that program, making it best suited to zones 6-9 (Georgia, the Carolinas, and similar Southeastern climates) rather than the most mild-winter Gulf Coast sites; self-fertile.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Julyprince is self-fruitful and bears large, very round, firm yellow freestone fruit that ripens around the same time as the older standard Redglobe. Bred by the USDA-ARS fruit breeding program at Byron, Georgia and released in 2008, Julyprince was selected for outstanding fruit size and firmness that holds up well to Southeastern growing conditions and handling. Thin fruit early to improve size, and expect the tree to perform best where winters reliably deliver enough chilling for a Georgia-adapted peach — gardeners on the immediate Gulf Coast should pair it with a lower-chill selection as insurance in mild winters.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Byron, GA Fruit and Tree Nut Research
Clemson Cooperative Extension HGIC — Peach Variety: Julyprince
University of Georgia Extension — Home Garden Peaches

common_name: Scarletprince Peach (USDA-ARS Byron Georgia Firm Yellow Freestone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Scarletprince was released in 2004 by USDA-ARS at Byron, Georgia for moderate bacterial-spot resistance and attractive, very firm fruit ripening in the Redglobe season; best adapted to zones 6-9; self-fertile.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Scarletprince is self-fruitful and produces attractive, very firm, yellow-fleshed freestone fruit with good moderate resistance to bacterial spot, a common foliage and fruit disease in the humid Southeast. Released by the USDA-ARS breeding program at Byron, Georgia in 2004, it was bred specifically to give Southeastern growers a firm, well-colored peach that ripens alongside the older Redglobe standard and ships and stores well. Thin fruit after bloom to improve size and sweetness, and prune to an open center for airflow.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Byron, GA Fruit and Tree Nut Research

common_name: Modesto Apricot (California's Classic All-Purpose Low-Chill Apricot)

planting.note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Modesto needs only about 400 chill hours or less, among the lowest requirements of any widely sold apricot, making it a strong candidate for zone 7-9 gardens including the Gulf South; self-fertile.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Modesto is self-fruitful and needs no second tree. For decades it was the top commercial apricot grown around Modesto, California for its reliable, all-purpose freestone fruit — sweet, aromatic, and good fresh, dried, or canned — and its early bloom combined with a chill requirement of 400 hours or less has made it a favorite recommendation for mild-winter gardens where classic high-chill apricots like Moorpark bloom unreliably. Thin fruit after natural drop to improve size, and site it away from late-frost pockets since its early bloom can be caught by a late cold snap; harvest in late June in most areas when fruit is fully orange and slightly soft.
sources: Dave Wilson Nursery — Apricot Variety Database

common_name: Debbie's Gold Apricot (Cold-Hardy Self-Fertile Prairie Apricot)
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Debbie's Gold is self-fertile and does not require a pollinizer. Selected from Prunus armeniaca var. sibirica seedling stock by Aubin Nurseries of Carman, Manitoba and introduced in 1980, it was bred for extreme cold hardiness rather than low chill — withstanding winter temperatures well below zero — and is considered one of the sweetest, least tart of the hardy prairie apricots. Fruit is medium-sized, golden-yellow, and freestone, ripening in late August; grow it where high-chill apricots are the limiting factor rather than where winters are too mild, and prune to control its vigorous, spreading habit.
sources: Aubin Nurseries — Prairie Fruit Introductions
North Dakota State University Extension — Hardy Fruit for the Northern Plains

common_name: Seneca Plum (Extra-Large Fresh-Eating New York European Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Seneca requires a European-plum pollinizer and about 800 chill hours, putting it outside true low-chill range and best suited to zones 4-9; not recommended for the mildest Gulf Coast winters.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and provide a compatible European plum pollinizer for a full crop. Introduced in 1972 by the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Seneca was bred to combine the large size and purple-red skin of a European plum with a fresh-eating character rather than the dense, drying-plum texture typical of many prune-type cultivars, yielding fruit that can weigh up to 3 ounces with rich amber flesh. Thin fruit for size, and expect a September harvest; the tree needs a real winter chill to perform well, so gardeners in the Deep South should choose a lower-chill Japanese or Japanese-American hybrid plum instead.
sources: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station (Cornell) — Fruit Variety Releases
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Growing Plums in the Home Garden
University of Georgia Extension — Home Garden Plums

common_name: Mariposa Plum (Heart-Shaped Red-Fleshed Low-Chill Japanese Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Mariposa needs only about 250 chill hours and a Japanese-plum pollinizer such as Santa Rosa, making it a strong choice for zone 6-10 gardens including the Gulf South.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and site a Santa Rosa or other bloom-compatible Japanese plum nearby for pollination. A heart-shaped, purple-skinned, vivid red-fleshed heirloom plum with sweet, juicy flavor, Mariposa (sometimes sold as Improved Satsuma) is one of the lower-chill named Japanese plums widely available in commerce, requiring only around 250 hours of winter chilling. This low chill requirement, combined with good heat tolerance, makes it well suited to Gulf Coast gardens where many standard plums bloom unevenly after mild winters; thin fruit after bloom and watch for brown rot in humid weather.

common_name: Formosa Plum (Burbank Heirloom Apricot-Flavored Low-Chill Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Formosa needs only about 300 chill hours and a compatible Japanese-plum pollinizer, making it suitable for zone 6-9 gardens including much of the Gulf South.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and provide a bloom-compatible Japanese plum such as Santa Rosa or Methley for pollination. Developed by Luther Burbank in the early 1900s and once marketed as one of the finest-flavored plums available, Formosa bears large, heart-shaped, yellow-skinned fruit blushed red with sweet flesh carrying a distinctive apricot-like note. Its relatively low chill requirement of around 300 hours has kept it in circulation among Southern and Gulf Coast growers long after many of Burbank's other introductions faded from commerce; thin fruit after bloom and prune to an open center to reduce brown rot pressure in humid climates.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Plum Fruit Facts

common_name: Craig's Crimson Cherry (Zaiger Low-Chill Self-Fertile Sweet Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Craig's Crimson needs only about 500-600 chill hours and is self-fruitful, a lower requirement than most sweet cherries though still higher than true Gulf Coast low-chill selections like Minnie Royal; best for zone 6-9.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Craig's Crimson is self-fruitful and does not require a second tree, though nearby bloom-compatible cherries can improve yield. A Zaiger Genetics introduction and natural semi-dwarf, it bears dark red to nearly black, firm, large cherries with a distinctive spicy-sweet flavor on a tree roughly two-thirds the size of a standard sweet cherry. Its late bloom helps it dodge spring frosts, and its comparatively modest 500-600 hour chill requirement extends sweet cherry growing into warmer zone 8-9 gardens than traditional Bing-type cultivars tolerate, though it still needs noticeably more winter chill than true ultra-low-chill selections bred specifically for the Gulf Coast.
sources: Dave Wilson Nursery — Cherry Variety Database
